passage:
Tuesday night. Hansa again today. Her pencil box spilled across the floor in maths and she just picked everything up, face blank. No fuss, no "Ma'am, help." She never asks. When Karthik tore her chart by accident, she said "It's fine" and turned to the window. Is it fine? I honestly don't know.
So I tried something small. At lunch I sat at the next desk, not beside her, marking books. I asked, "Glue stick or tape for your chart?" She chose tape. Then I just stayed there, marking. She fixed the chart and slid it an inch closer to my side of the desk.
Tomorrow: same time, same desk. No pushing.
Ishita

qa.q: What did Hansa choose to fix her chart?
qa.a: She chose tape.

qa.q: What might Hansa be feeling when she says "It's fine" and turns to the window?
qa.a: She may be upset about the torn chart but used to keeping it to herself.

qa.q: What small step did Ishita try, and why does it suit Hansa?
qa.a: Ishita sat at the next desk and offered a simple choice, giving steady company without pressure.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Hansa says "It's fine" after he tears her chart?
qa.a: Karthik might feel relieved, but also unsure whether Hansa is really okay, since she turns away.

grounding: A teacher's diary notes a child who never asks for help and seems fine during upsets, and tries a quiet check-in with a choice and steady presence.

passage: In the one-storey school at the edge of the sugarcane fields, Kamal sir had been watching Noor for weeks. When rain leaked through the roof onto her notebook, she dried it on her sleeve and said nothing. When other children crowded round him with questions, she sat back, sums done or not. He didn't call her out. Every morning he stopped by her bench: "Slate or notebook today?" Every afternoon he sat on the verandah step till the bus came, reading. After a month, Noor sat down two steps away. The next week, one step. One afternoon she held out her notebook. "Sir, this sum. I don't get it."

qa.q: Where did Kamal sir sit every afternoon?
qa.a: He sat on the verandah step till the bus came, reading.

qa.q: What might Noor be feeling when she dries her notebook and says nothing?
qa.a: She may be upset but unused to asking for help, so she keeps it to herself.

qa.q: Which of Kamal sir's choices helped Noor come closer, and why?
qa.a: He offered her small daily choices and was reliably there on the verandah, so she could approach at her own pace.

qa.q: What is it like for Noor to finally say "Sir, this sum"?
qa.a: It is likely a big, brave step for her, possible because Kamal sir has been steady for weeks.

grounding: A village teacher notices a self-contained girl, offers quiet choices and steady availability, and over weeks she comes closer to ask for help.

passage: In Ms Elif's third-grade class in Izmir, Ada never raised her hand for help. When her tower of blocks for the science project collapsed, she rebuilt it, face blank. When a classmate tore her drawing, she said, "It's fine," and started again. Elif noticed the pencil pressed hard enough to rip the new paper. She didn't ask "What's wrong?" in front of everyone. At the end of the day she left a note on Ada's desk: "I'm in the classroom at lunch on Tuesdays and Thursdays if you want to draw with me. Your choice." The first Tuesday the room stayed empty. On Thursday, Ada came in, sat two desks away and drew in silence.

qa.q: On which days did Ms Elif offer lunchtime drawing?
qa.a: Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Elif thinking when she saw the pencil ripping the paper?
qa.a: She was concerned, sensing that Ada was upset under her blank face and "It's fine".

qa.q: Which choice of Elif's worked, and why?
qa.a: A private note with a choice and steady times, because it gave Ada a safe way to come closer without pressure.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ada to walk in on Thursday?
qa.a: Ada probably felt cautious but curious, testing whether the offer was real by sitting two desks away.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a self-contained child and using a quiet, steady offer with a choice so the child can come closer.

passage: At the hostel school in Darjeeling, Tenzin-sir had taught Zeenat maths for two terms and never once seen her ask for help. When her mother's call was cancelled on visiting Sunday, she said, "Okay," and went to do her laundry. When she got a fraction sum wrong on the board, she erased it and stood still, face calm, till he moved on. So he stopped asking "Any doubts?" to the whole class. Instead, during practice, he stopped by her desk: "Want a hint, or want to try once more first?" She usually chose to try. By the second month she began leaving a small question mark in her notebook margin, where only he would see it.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do after her mother's call was cancelled?
qa.a: She said, "Okay," and went to do her laundry.

qa.q: What was Tenzin-sir thinking when Zeenat stood still after the wrong sum?
qa.a: He was concerned that she never asked for help and seemed fine even when upset, so he changed how he offered help.

qa.q: Why does offering a choice work better than asking the whole class for doubts?
qa.a: It lets Zeenat accept help privately and on her own terms, without being exposed.

qa.q: What does the small question mark show about how Zeenat feels?
qa.a: That she is beginning to trust Tenzin-sir enough to ask for help, in a way that feels safe to her.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher who notices a child who never asks for help and uses quiet check-ins and choices.

passage: I'm Ganga, the trainee teacher in Class 6-C this term, so mostly I watch. Nazia is the girl everyone calls "no trouble". She finishes her work, never asks anything, and when her group's poster got ripped on Monday she said, "It's okay," before anyone else spoke. But I noticed she didn't eat her lunch that day, and she picked at the edge of her sleeve all afternoon. I can't know what she felt. I tried not to crowd her. I asked, "Do you want to redo the poster at your desk or at the back table?" She chose the back table, which is near mine. The next day she sat there again without being asked, and once, very quietly, asked me how to spell "volcano".

qa.q: Where did Nazia choose to redo the poster?
qa.a: At the back table.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling on noticing the uneaten lunch and picked sleeve?
qa.a: Ganga felt concerned, sensing Nazia might be upset despite saying "It's okay", but was careful not to assume.

qa.q: What made Ganga's approach work?
qa.a: Offering a simple choice instead of a demand and being steadily nearby, which let Nazia come closer.

qa.q: How might Nazia see the back table the next day?
qa.a: Nazia seems to find it a safe spot near a steady adult, where asking a small question feels possible.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a child who looks fine during upsets and offering choices and steady availability.

passage:
Week one: Deepika Ma'am noticed that Lalit never raised his hand for help, even when his sums were wrong. When Arun tore his notebook, Lalit shrugged and kept writing. She wondered what the shrug was holding in.
Week three: Instead of calling him to her desk, she crouched by his bench. "Want to try the next one with me, or on your own first?" He chose "own first". She said, "I'll be at the window if you want me."
Week six: During a thunderstorm, the class got noisy. Lalit walked over to the window and stood next to her, not speaking. After a minute he said, "Ma'am, I didn't get question four." She smiled, careful not to make a fuss, and pulled up a chair.

qa.q: What did Arun do to Lalit's notebook?
qa.a: Arun tore his notebook.

qa.q: What was Deepika Ma'am feeling about Lalit's shrug in week one?
qa.a: She felt concerned and curious about what the shrug was holding in, since he never asked for help.

qa.q: Which of Deepika Ma'am's steps helped Lalit come closer?
qa.a: Giving him a choice instead of a demand and saying she would be at the window, so he knew where help was without pressure.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Lalit to ask about question four?
qa.a: It was probably a big, slightly nervous step for Lalit, easier because she stayed calm and didn't make a fuss.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a self-contained child and, over weeks, using quiet check-ins, choices and steady availability until he comes closer.
